chapters.title: The Business of Cash and Carry
chapters.summary: Mahendra Ramsinghani frames venture as cash and carry where limited partners carry risk for ten years and general partners carry portfolio for five before they see carry. The opening metaphor from a veteran LP is that VC is the only business where you buy high, carry for a decade, and pray the carrying works. The chapter quantifies the 2 and 20 model with a waterfall illustration: one hundred million fund, two percent management fee fifteen million over life, invested capital eighty-five million, hurdle eight percent, and 80-20 split above hurdle after return of capital — a math that reveals fees alone can be most of early distributions if exits delay. The illustration shows pie slices where fees consume eighteen percent of commitments before a single exit. The cash and carry tension is lived in the 2020-21 vintage where hedge funds and sovereigns flooded private markets, compressing carry for those who raised at precrisis multiples. The chapter introduces the archetype of the qualified purchaser and accredited investor gates that define LP universe, reproduced as a regulatory table. An anecdote from a first-time solo GP who assumed carry meant salary, only to learn he pays tax on unrealized gains if he takes early carry, drives home why structure matters before strategy. The chapter ends with a carry sensitivity curve plotting TVPI at 2.5 needed to produce meaningful GP wealth after fees, explaining why top quartile matters disproportionately — median 1.8 TVPI yields modest carry while 3.2 creates generational. The carry table becomes the lens for every later fundraising and portfolio chapter, reminding readers that venture is not stock picking but fund economics where carry, fees, and vintage dictate behavior. chapters.title: Why Choose a Career in VC & Attributes of Successful VCs
chapters.summary: Ramsinghani juxtaposes romanticized career choice — access, pattern recognition, founder support — with attritional reality documented via interviews with fifty GPs and LPs. The why chapter cites an early-career VC who left Morgan Stanley because he wanted to build rather than advise, then discovered that building means carrying founders through flat rounds and layoffs where the LP asks why carry is low. The attributes chapter distills what LPs say they back after reading dozens of due diligence memos: intellectual curiosity that compounds, network generosity where the VC returns calls within 24 hours even when not lead, and probabilistic thinking that survives power law. An illustration replicates a LP scorecard weighting references at thirty percent above track record because character predicts behavior at failure. The anecdote that anchors attributes is the almost hiring of a Stanford GSB star who aced case study but failed reference check when a founder said he ghosted after passing, costing the firm the allocation. Another attribute is dealing with enemies accumulating, Charles Hudson's phrase, where today's pass becomes tomorrow's competitor, requiring gracious decline notes that preserve optionality. The chapter contrasts the making of a VC via apprenticeship — analyst to partner in twelve years at Accel — versus operator to VC in three, showing both can work if generational transfer is mentored. The illustration maps career pathways as lattice versus ladder. The closing curve plots VC satisfaction versus portfolio age, showing trough at year six when fund is deployed but exits are zero, the moment career faith is tested. Together these chapters tell readers that choosing VC is choosing to be measured on a decade delay, and attributes are not brilliance but behaviors observable in references and decline etiquette. chapters.title: Welcome to the Land of Ad-Venture & Developing Your Investment Career
chapters.summary: Land of Ad-Venture reframes Venture with capital V as adventure with risk. The chapter introduces biases and cognitive traps — availability from recent unicorns, anchoring on last round valuation, confirmation where warm introductions filter, and loss aversion where partners hold mediocre winners to avoid realizing failure — illustrated as a bias wheel where each spoke points to a deal stage. A de-risking exercise from the book invites partners to pre-mortem a term sheet: assume the company fails and list three reasons why, forcing disconfirming evidence before investing. Developing Your Investment Career then operationalizes de-risking via daily habits: write a one-page point of view on a market, publish it, and let it attract founders who disagree, creating deal flow through intellectual honesty. The anecdote of a Chicago associate who wrote on cold chain logistics and sourced three logistics deals from that single post proves the method. The chapter details skills requisite — sourcing, picking, winning, nurturing, exiting — and argues picking is only twenty percent of time while sourcing and winning are sixty, an allocation pie that surprises new VCs who romanticize picking. Illustration maps time allocation versus outcome contribution and shows mismatch. The skill progression illustration plots from analyst note-taking to partner board leading as three loops where each loop adds judgment load. The chapter's tool is the investment thesis canvas where market, product, and business model analysis converge; a sample canvas for future of work shows bottom-up TAM where number of freelancers times spend replaces top-down billion dollar claims. Together these chapters teach that adventure rewards structured process, not gut, and career develops by publishing point of view, pre-morteming biases, and allocating time to sourcing and winning rather than only diligence perfection. chapters.title: A Business Where Enemies Accumulate & Generational Transfer
chapters.summary: The title phrase from Charles Hudson captures VC's small-world gravity: you will compete with yesterday's co-investor for today's hot round. The chapter tells a story of a 2014 co-led Series A where both firms promised pro rata, then one blocked the other's pro rata in Series B by using pay-to-play, an illustration shows cap table where blocking washes out the early partner, and the relationship never recovered. Ramsinghani lists enemy accumulation vectors — blocking, information leakage from board, hiring portfolio talent — and advises writing decline emails that compliment team and leave door open, reproduced as templated note. The generational transfer chapter confronts the firm's mortality: partners age, carry vests over four years, and LPs who backed the founding pair fear the bench. The case is Andreessen Horowitz's formal generational plan where Scott Kupor's foreword frames evolution, versus firms that imploded when a founder left with fund name and no succession agreement, illustrated as two succession timelines. An anecdote recounts a seventy-year-old founding GP who refused to name successor until LP due diligence forced it, causing his final fund to be half subscribed. The illustration maps vesting and step-up: new partner earns ten percent of carry in Fund III, thirty percent in Fund IV if performance permits. The chapter's tool is partnership ethos session where partners write values before strategy — an ethos culture workshop template reproduced — because values decide who gets to stay. The synthesis is that enemies accumulate quickly and succession fails slowly unless ethos and vesting are explicit early, not at liquidity event. Readers learn to keep a relationship ledger and to negotiate succession before fundraising, because LPs diligence team continuity more than strategy decks. chapters.title: LP Universe & Fund of Funds
chapters.summary: The LP universe chapter taxonomizes capital sources with diligence implications. Endowments like Yale chase illiquidity premium and can commit to ten-year lock-up, illustrated as horizon bar where endowments sit at decade; public pensions like CalPERS need nearer liquidity and face political scrutiny that makes VC pacing difficult; sovereign wealth funds like ADIA bring scale but sovereign objectives that may press for co-invest; family offices write smaller checks quickly but need education on vintage risk; corporate venture like GV offers strategic value but conflicts when portfolio competes; fund of funds offers diversification for small LPs at double fees, a gate relevant for first-time managers. A table maps each LP type to check size median, decision speed in months, and care about impact. The LPs of Choice fund of funds chapter explains why FOFs, mocked for fees, actually serve first-time funds best: FOFs absorb diligence cost and give credibility signal, illustrated as a trust cascade where one reputable FOF commitment unlocks three pensions. The anecdote is a Minneapolis FOF manager who seeded a solo GP with three million after reading his cold chain point of view, then introduced him to two pensions, catalyzing twenty-five million close. The illustration traces that introduction chain. The chapter also warns that FOFs demand most-favored-nation terms and co-invest rights, and that fundraising roadshow must tailor story per LP — endowments want edge via sourcing, pensions want risk management and reporting discipline, corporates want strategic fit. The diligence lens introduced here is how LPs conduct fund diligence, previewed as team, strategy, and performance analysis — a Venn where only overlap gets allocated. Together these chapters equip GPs to target LPs who fit their fund size and horizon rather than blasting all LPs with same deck, a classic error that wastes a year. chapters.title: How LPs Conduct Fund Due Diligence & Investment Strategy and Team
chapters.summary: LPs diligence team and strategy before performance because past performance is noisy in venture. The chapter reproduces a due diligence questionnaire where the first page asks who sourced the top five deals and who said no to the five best passes, probing attribution. An illustration shows team diligence matrix scoring partner on sourcing, picking, winning, nurturing, and exiting separately, revealing whether a star was carried. Investment strategy definition then forces choice: seed versus Series A, sector versus generalist, geography, check size, and portfolio construction math. A fund size illustration shows why a fifty million fund writing 500k checks can own thirteen positions and still follow-on while a 300 million fund writing same checks would be under-invested — size must match opportunity zone. Performance analysis chapter ahead is previewed with DPI, TVPI, and IRR definitions where IRR without DPI at year eight is red flag, a pitfalls table. The narrative anecdote is a fund that marketed IRR of thirty percent at year three on marked-up unicorns but had DPI of 0.1, which LPs flagged by asking for realized versus unrealized attribution, causing the manager to restate. The team diligence illustration also maps allocation of carry and vesting, the part LPs inspect after team. The ethos culture chapter is previewed as values interview where LPs call back-channel references asking how partners behaved in down round and departure, unpredictable in data room but visible in behavior. For emerging managers, the lesson is to define strategy narrow enough to be diligence-able but wide enough to own winners, and to bring attribution truthfully because LPs will call founders you did not list. chapters.title: Fund Size, Portfolio Construction, Performance, and Terms
chapters.summary: Fund size and portfolio construction is arithmetic with consequences. The chapter's central model plots fund size on x-axis versus expected ownership at exit needed to return fund: a 200 million fund needs 1 percent of a unicorn that exits at 2 billion, while a 50 million fund needs 4 percent at 500 million, illustrated as hyperbola. The construction table shows thirteen to eighteen companies as optimal for seed, allowing reserve for follow-on at 60/40 initial to follow-on split; fewer than ten concentrates failure risk above power law, more than twenty-five dilutes ownership below conviction. Performance analysis then decodes benchmarks: Cambridge Associates and Preqin quartiles where top quartile vintage 2015 TVPI 2.8 versus median 1.7, an illustration maps quartile persistence where top quartile GPs repeat at forty percent. Terms of fund investment translate construction to economics: management fee step-down from two percent on commitments to two on invested after investment period, recycle provisions, and management fee offsets from director fees and monitoring fees, reproduced as term sheet excerpt. The venture firm's ethos culture and values chapter ties terms to behavior — high fees without recycle incentivize asset gathering over performance, illustrated as fee drag where ten-year fees at three percent consume thirty percent of commitments. The case is a fund that raised 400 million when opportunity was 150 million and later showed bottom quartile because ownership was diluted and fee load high. The anecdote of a manager who volunteered fee waiver after year seven to align with LPs and then earned loyalty for Fund II is highlighted. The closing illustration is a portfolio construction simulator where GP inputs fund size, check size, ownership target, and expected failures, and sees DPI sensitivity, a tool readers can replicate to choose size before roadshow rather than after LPs ask. chapters.title: Raising Your First Fund & The Fundraising Roadshow
chapters.summary: Raising a first fund is the book's most tactical section, written for solo GPs. The chapter quantifies why LPs seek first-time funds — top quartile first funds outperform median second funds where hunger is higher and size smaller — a persistence chart shows first-time top quartile at 3.1 TVPI versus second-time at 2.6. Then it flips to why LPs fear them — key person risk and no realized DPI — so the homework is to manufacture credibility: warehouse three to five deals on personal capital, show markup and governance, and bring founder references who validate nurturing, not just picking, illustrated as warehouse track record sheet. The fundraising roadshow chapter maps the process as 100 meetings to 20 second meetings to 5 diligence to 2 closes, illustrated as funnel with durations where average cycle is nine months and advice is to start at 30 percent of target, not zero. An anecdote recounts a first-time GP who targeted endowments first and failed for six months, then pivoted to family offices and FOFs and closed in four months after one credible FOF anchor, a sequence diagram shows ordering. Why LPs seek first-time funds chapter adds contrarian math: LPs allocated to first-time vintage 2010-15 earned 400 bps above experienced, because fee leverage and small size overweight winners. The roadshow deck structure reproduced is problem, point of view, sourcing edge, attribution, construction, and alignment — six slides where LPs decide in first twelve minutes. The chapter ends with why LPs conduct fund due diligence chapter preview repeated, emphasizing that first-time diligence is character diligence where LPs call references you did not list to test integrity. Together these chapters tell first-time managers to warehouse, sequence FOF first, and sell attribution truthfully, because LPs are buying the next ten years of behavior not the last three years of markup. chapters.title: Sourcing Investment Opportunities & Due Diligence Cheat Sheet
chapters.summary: Sourcing is portrayed as systematic hunting where inbound is brand and outbound is hustle. The chapter lists channels — warm introductions from portfolio, cold outreach to researchers publishing on arXiv, community building via office hours, and platform where a16z's content engine attracts founders who disagree — an illustration maps inbound versus outbound mix where top quartile firms are forty percent outbound. The cheat sheet condenses diligence to one-page canvas: team, product, market, business model, and terms, reproduced as checklist with red flags per box. The diligence chapter deepens each box: team assessment uses intangible scores on coachability and resilience tested via references who saw the founder after failure, not just success; market, product, and business model analysis uses bottom-up TAM and magic versus logic tests where magic is ten-times better product and logic is must-have versus nice-to-have, illustrated as two-axis where magic plus must-have wins. The chapter's anecdote is a GP who sourced via reading FDA 510k filings for device approvals before press, contacting founders same day, winning deal where inbound firms arrived two months later. The due diligence cheat sheet table shows timeline: one week to canvas, two weeks to customer calls, one week to terms — four weeks total where speed is edge but skipping customer calls kills. The closing illustration is a sourcing CRM screenshot where every founder gets follow-up note within 48 hours, proving that system beats memory. Together sourcing and diligence are framed as portfolio management begins at sourcing quality, because you cannot diligence your way out of weak pipeline. chapters.title: Terms, Closing, and Structure of the Term Sheet
chapters.summary: Terms are where price meets protection. The terms and conditions apply chapter lists price, liquidation preference, participation, anti-dilution, pay-to-play, vesting, and protective provisions, illustrated as term sheet excerpt where 1x non-participating preferred with broad-based weighted average anti-dilution is standard. The structure of the term sheet chapter animates negotiation: buy low sell high chapter frames entry valuation discipline where paying 2x for ten-times outcome kills fund return, a entry multiple versus outcome chart shows required ownership math. The convertible note as quasi-security chapter is updated: SAFE and convertible notes defer pricing but carry valuation cap, discount, and pro rata rights that are quasi-security, illustrated as cap table at conversion where uncapped note dilutes founders badly. An anecdote recounts a founder who took uncapped note with twenty percent discount, then raised at low valuation where note converted at 20 percent discount to low price, wiping founder — a cautionary tale where discount without cap is trap. The closing process chapter covers confirmatory diligence, disclosure schedules, and legal closing where unanimity on closing conditions prevents last-minute walk-away, illustrated as closing checklist of employment agreements, IP assignment, and compliance. The chapter's buy low sell high discipline ties back to cash and carry — carry is determined at entry price, not exit optimism — and the illustration shows that a 50 percent lower entry price equals one extra unicorn in portfolio effect. Together terms chapters teach that term sheet is governance not just price, and closing is disclosure hygiene that prevents litigation that later costs carry. chapters.title: Serving on Boards, Value Creation, and Board Challenges
chapters.summary: Board service is the art of being helpful without being helicopter. Serving on boards chapter opens with the first board meeting template reproduced where founders report KPIs, cash runway, and asks, and directors ask questions not give answers — illustrated as agenda where founder talks seventy percent. Board culture and orientation chapter maps culture to high trust low hierarchy where independent directors challenge, illustrated as trust versus hierarchy two-by-two. Value creation chapter reframes let me know how I can be helpful from platitude to playbook: introductions to five customers, recruiting bar raising, and follow-on signaling — an illustration traces how a16z's signal in Series B raised price but also attracted talent because signal is endorsement. The challenges in the boardroom chapter catalogues common failures: founder-CEO who is product genius but sales avoidant, board that micromanages product roadmap, and the down round where pay-to-play forces choice between dilution and abandonment, illustrated as pay-to-play decision tree. An anecdote recounts a board that replaced CEO too late after two missed quarters where the dashboard had shown sales cycle lengthening but board deferred, costing the company. The chapter's tool is board effectiveness survey where directors rate preparation, engagement, and conflict, reproduced as scorecard. Together these chapters argue that value creation is measured in customer introductions closed and hires made, not board attendance, and challenges are mitigated by trust culture and early CEO transition when dashboard signals persist two quarters. chapters.title: Exit Strategies, Acquisitions, IPO, and Secondary Sales
chapters.summary: Exits are liquidity events where champagne is cheaper than carry calculations. The exit strategies chapter quantifies power law where most returns come from one or two portfolio winners — a histogram shows ten investments where one at 50x returns fund while seven fail — so exit discipline matters disproportionately on the one. Acquisitions chapter details M&A prep: banker selection, earnout where twenty percent of consideration contingent on revenue, and retention where founders vest eighteen months post-close, illustrated as earnout timeline where missing target halves payout. The IPO chapter walks through underwriter selection, S-1 drafting, roadshow, greenshoe where underwriter oversells fifteen percent to stabilize, and lock-up where insiders hold 180 days, illustrated as IPO timeline over six months with pricing at 3 a.m. The secondary sales chapter covers secondaries where early employees sell to late-stage funds, a liquidity path when IPO window shut, illustrated as secondaries volume chart rising after 2018 when public window narrowed. The closing note adds a new chapter on your own exit strategies where GP secondary and fund continuation vehicles are explained — illustrated as continuation fund diagram where LPs can roll or redeem, a path that now provides liquidity without forcing company sale. An anecdote recounts a founder who rejected early acquisition at 100 million, pursued IPO at 800 million, and succeeded because board protected runway, contrasting with a fire sale at 40 million when runway fell to six months. The synthesis is that exits are where venture's patience either pays in ten-year carry or is wasted by selling too early when power law requires letting the one winner run to public market scale.
